bibliographic.authors: Cheng-Yi Wang, Biing-Suan Lim, Ya-Hui Wang and Yuh-Chin T. Huang
bibliographic.affiliations: Cardinal Tien Hospital / Fu-Jen Catholic University, New Taipei City; Duke University Medical Center, Durham NC
bibliographic.title: Identification of High Personal PM2.5 Exposure during Real Time Commuting in the Taipei Metropolitan Area
bibliographic.volumeIssuePages: Atmosphere 2021, 12(3), 396; 15 pages. Received 4 Feb 2021, accepted 12 Mar 2021, published 19 Mar 2021
bibliographic.funding: 'This research received no external funding.' (p.12). Acknowledgments thank Cardinal Tien Hospital for 'logistic and funding support' (p.13). No conflict of interest declared. IRB: Not applicable.
bibliographic.openAccess: CC BY 4.0 (p.1). Raw data 'available upon request' (p.13).

studyDesign: Observational descriptive study of personal PM2.5 during commuting in greater Taipei (Taipei City + New Taipei City), April-July 2019 (p.4), months with the lowest ambient PM2.5 in northern Taiwan (p.3). Five volunteers carried one Temtop P600 laser light-scattering detector (range 0-999 ug/m3, 0.1 resolution, time resolution 1 min) at mid-chest height, sensor facing away from the body (p.3); 3 readings per measurement averaged; negative/invalid points removed; room-air check (5-10 ug/m3) before each trip; low-wind conditions only. Not calibrated against FEM-Grimm or TEOM; authors cite a manufacturer-sensor field test (adjusted = 0.678 x measured + 3.298, R2 0.915, about 30% downward) but report all results unadjusted. Modes: walking (sidewalks, night market), MRT (34 trips, 30-90 min, rush and off-peak), air-conditioned buses, motorcycle (3 trips, measured only when idle e.g. at red lights, p.4), private car (5 trips, AC, recirculation, windows closed). Ambient comparison: nearest Taiwan EPA stations (inlet 15-20 m per p.4; 10-15 m per pp.2, 5, 12), beta-ray/TEOM. Statistics: median and range or mean +/- SD; Wilcoxon rank-sum multiple comparison, JMP 13, p<0.05. Walking and bus trip counts, hours per mode and per-volunteer split are not stated. Per-mode n are individual measurements, not independent people or trips. Only PM2.5 was measured.

findings.claim: Pedestrians on city sidewalks in greater Taipei had a median hand-held PM2.5 of 40 ug/m3, with a very wide range.
findings.value: Walking on sidewalks: median 40 ug/m3, range 10-275, n = 216 measurements
findings.quote: The median PM2.5 concentration when walking on the sidewalks of the city streets was 40 µg/m3 (range 10–275 µg/m3 , n = 216 measurements)
findings.significance: Reference group for other comparisons; no CI. Mean not given.
findings.caveats: Uncalibrated low-cost sensor, authors say it overestimates by about 30% (p.3); five volunteers; April-July 2019 only (lowest-pollution season); no breakdown into intersection vs non-intersection in the aggregate. Fig. 8 labels this group 'Roadside'.
findings.useOnSite: Walking along Taipei streets in spring-summer 2019, a hand-held low-cost sensor recorded a median of 40 ug/m3 PM2.5 (range 10-275); the authors say the sensor probably reads about 30% high.
findings.checkerNote: Quote, n, units and page verified in text and Fig. 8.

findings.claim: Ambient PM2.5 at government stations during the study was low.
findings.value: Study-period station values 2-38 ug/m3, median 14; monthly averages Apr 19, May 14, Jun 12, Jul 12 ug/m3 (10 stations)
findings.quote: ranged from 2–38 µg/m3 with a median of 14 µg/m3 . Monthly average PM2.5 concentrations for April, May, June, and July of 2019 ... were 19, 14, 12 and 12 µg/m3
findings.caveats: Station inlets are elevated; measured by different methods (beta-ray/TEOM).
findings.useOnSite: Official station readings in the study period had a median of 14 ug/m3.
findings.checkerNote: Verified p.4.

findings.claim: Simultaneous street-level hand-held readings were only weakly related to nearby EPA station values and sat above them.
findings.value: 24 paired measurements, five stations: S = 0.958 M + 23.353, R2 = 0.275, p = 0.006 (S street, M station, ug/m3). Fig. 2: street values about 12-55 against station values about 2-22 (read from figure)
findings.quote: The linear equation is S = 0.958 M + 23.353 ... (R2 = 0.275, p = 0.006). The poor association was likely due to the difference in the measurement ... at a height of 10–15 m and those measured at the ground level.
findings.significance: p = 0.006 as printed (it is not stated whether this is for the slope or the model); R2 0.275 is weak. No CI.
findings.caveats: The authors attribute the gap to station height and method (light scattering vs TEOM) and sensor overestimate, not to a quantified traffic increment. The height attribution rests on a 10-20x figure cited from another paper [30]. Ratios are not reported by the authors. Station height is stated as 15-20 m on p.4 but 10-15 m on pp.2, 5, 12.
findings.useOnSite: At street level near stations, readings exceeded station values (regression intercept about 23 ug/m3), though the authors caution that height, instrument type and sensor bias all contribute.
findings.checkerNote: Equation, R2, p, n=24 pairs verified; Fig. 2 axes read from the PDF page (street 12.5-55, station 2-22).

findings.claim: In the example trips, personal readings were several times the simultaneous station values in most legs.
findings.value: Motorcycle trip 29 Apr 2019 (Fig. 7): readings while riding about 60-75 vs stations Datong 20, Songshan 17. Bus trip 1 May (Fig. 6): personal 15-35 vs stations 4-10. Underground MRT trip 11 June (Fig. 4): ride 70-95 vs stations Xindian 2, Guting 6. Walk 10 Apr (Table 1): ambient 21 vs 57.5-100. Walk 27 Apr (Table 3): ambient 5 vs 30-700
findings.locator: Figs 4-7 red dots; Tables 1-3; Discussion p.12
findings.quote: Also note that most PM2.5 measurements during commuting were higher than the ambient concentrations (Figures 3–5).
findings.significance: n/a; single illustrative trips, no formal ratio.
findings.caveats: Hand-picked example trips; no ratio or difference statistic is computed in the paper; uncorrected sensor. Several example trips also include indoor readings well above the station value (see added finding on indoor baseline).
findings.useOnSite: In the paper's worked example trips, readings while stopped on the motorcycle (about 60-75) were roughly three to four times the nearest station values (17-20); this ratio is our arithmetic, not the paper's, and uses unadjusted sensor values.
findings.checkerNote: Reader gave motorcycle personal 55-75; in Fig. 7 the 55 is the final indoor point, readings on the ride are about 60-75 (paper's overall motorcycle range 60-105). The quoted sentence is on p.12 (Discussion), not pp.5-9, and the paper cites Figures 3-5.

findings.claim: In one example walk, concentrations rose at intersections of major roads; the authors link this to traffic exhaust and road dust.
findings.value: 10 Apr 2019 (sunny, 26 C, RH 69%, ambient 21): alley 65; intersection of major roads 95 and 100; hospital 1st floor 65; office 57.5 ug/m3 (Table 1)
findings.quote: Note the concentration rose at the intersections of major roads. The concentration increased at the intersection in part because of the increased automobile traffic that generated more exhaust and road dust.
findings.caveats: Attribution is the authors' interpretation, not a source apportionment. 'Automobile traffic' is not split into cars vs scooters; no red-light or crosswalk analysis. Indoor readings in the same walk (65, 57.5) were far above the ambient 21.
findings.useOnSite: In one documented walk, readings at major-road intersections (95-100 ug/m3) were higher than in an alley (65); the authors attribute this to traffic exhaust and road dust.
findings.checkerNote: Table 1 values and quote verified on p.5-6.

findings.claim: In a second example walk, roadside bus stops and crossing a road read higher than in front of the hospital or inside the home.
findings.value: Table 2 (10 Apr; text: rainy, 24 C, RH 77%, ambient 5): in front of hospital 24; bus stop by major road 36 and 22.5; crossing the road 45; walking by a temple 85; family courtyard 42.5; inside house 20 ug/m3
findings.quote: Crossing the road | 45
findings.caveats: Tiny sample; 45 while crossing is not far above 36 at the bus stop; Table 1 and Table 2 are both dated 10 April but described as sunny (ambient 21) and rainy (ambient 5).
findings.useOnSite: One walk recorded 45 ug/m3 while crossing a road, versus 20 indoors at home.
findings.checkerNote: Table 2 values and date discrepancy verified.

findings.claim: The highest walking values the paper documents came from temple surroundings (incense burning) and food-stall cooking, not from traffic.
findings.value: Near temple: mean 588 +/- 271 ug/m3 (SD); underground food court: 405 +/- 238; Table 3: outside Mazu temple 700, fried oyster cake stand 400, fried chicken patty stand 150, grilled steak stand 95 (the three stalls are shaded as inside the underground food court); Table 2 walking by a temple on a rainy day: 85
findings.quote: Average PM2.5 concentrations near the temple and inside the underground food court were 588 ± 271 µg/m3 and 405 ± 238 µg/m3 respectively.
findings.significance: Abstract: p<0.0001 vs walking (the Results text does not itself give this p). n for the means not stated.
findings.caveats: Not scooter-related. Temple readings range widely (85 in Table 2, 700 in Table 3). The means 588 and 405 cannot be reproduced from Table 3 alone (Table 3 has one temple reading and three food-court readings), so they come from more readings than are tabulated. The sidewalk set's maximum of 275 is below 700 and 400, so these appear to be separate from the 216 sidewalk measurements, but the paper does not say.
findings.useOnSite: The paper's highest street-level readings came from temple incense and stir-fry stalls, not traffic, so the site should not attribute extreme peaks to scooters.
findings.checkerNote: Added Table 2 temple value, derivability caveat, and the page of the incense/cooking attribution (p.11; the reader's answer 3 said p.10).

findings.claim: The paper does not say where or why the 275 ug/m3 walking maximum occurred.
findings.value: Walking max 275 ug/m3; Fig. 8 roadside box plot shows outliers near 275, about 250-260 (two to three points), about 160 and 135-150 (read from figure)
findings.quote: (range 10–275 µg/m3 , n = 216 measurements)
findings.caveats: No text links the 275 peak, or the other outliers, to any source, place or time. Whole-text search finds no mention of scooters, smoking, cigarettes or fuel.
findings.useOnSite: The paper reports a maximum of 275 ug/m3 while walking but does not identify its cause.
findings.checkerNote: Fig. 8 outliers checked on the PDF page; text search confirmed no source named.

findings.claim: In the Shilin walk (Table 3), readings at ordinary street intersections were modest (30-50) and the large values were at the temple and food stalls; the intersection by the night market read 80.
findings.value: Table 3 (27 Apr, ambient 5): intersections A 30, B 40, I 50, J 30; night-market/Jihe Rd intersection H 80; road by night market G 85; night market entrance E 40; Danan Rd 35 ug/m3
findings.quote: H (night market/Jihe Rd Intersection) | 80
findings.caveats: Single walk, 12 readings; the text's reference to 'time points 15:20 and 15:25' does not match Table 3 times (16:32-17:30). The weather for this walk is not stated in the text; the Fig. 5 MRT trip on the same date (27 April) was partly cloudy, 23 C, RH 84%.
findings.useOnSite: On one walk with ambient 5, ordinary intersections read 30-50 ug/m3, so not every intersection is high.
findings.checkerNote: Reader's 'rainy-day style walk' is unsupported: the paper gives no weather for Table 3. Reader's claim range '30-80' mixed the night-market intersection (80) with ordinary ones; reworded.

findings.claim: PM2.5 measured while the motorcycle was idle (for example waiting for red lights) was about twice the walking median.
findings.value: Motorcycle: median 75 ug/m3, range 60-105, n = 21 measurements from 3 trips, p = 0.0011 vs walking (text); abstract says p<0.0001
findings.quote: A total of three motorcycle trips were taken. The median PM2.5 concentration was 75 µg/m3 (range: 60–105 µg/m3 , n = 21 measurements, p = 0.0011 vs. walking).
findings.significance: p = 0.0011 (Wilcoxon rank-sum vs walking); no CI. The abstract's p<0.0001 conflicts with the text's 0.0011.
findings.caveats: Only 3 trips, 21 readings; measured only when the motorcycle was idle (p.4). The motorcycle's fuel/engine type is not stated. Fig. 7 shows the 29 Apr trip with about 11 on-ride points. Readings are not independent.
findings.useOnSite: Measured at stops on three motorcycle trips (21 readings), the rider's median was 75 ug/m3, about twice the walking median of 40.
findings.checkerNote: Claim reworded from 'waiting at lights' to 'idle, e.g. red lights', since p.11 says 'different stops'. Numbers confirmed.

findings.claim: Motorcycle readings were taken only while stationary, e.g. at red lights, so they do not represent riding in motion.
findings.value: Idle-only measurement protocol
findings.quote: For safety reasons, PM2.5 concentrations were measured only when the motorcycle was idle, for example, waiting for red lights.
findings.caveats: Authors guess moving exposure is 'probably' lower (p.11), unmeasured. Fig. 7 plots a continuous line across the trip, but Methods say only idle readings were taken; the line is interpolation between sparse points (e.g. no points between 18:26 and 18:44).
findings.useOnSite: Motorcycle values are from stops such as red lights, not from moving traffic.
findings.checkerNote: Verified; Fig. 7 gap checked on PDF.

findings.claim: The authors reason that motorcyclists ride in car lanes, so they get more direct exposure to exhaust from cars and motorcycles than pedestrians or bus riders.
findings.value: Qualitative statement; no measurement of lane position or leading vehicle
findings.quote: In Taiwan, motorcyclists frequently ride on the car lanes. Therefore, they would be exposed to exhaust from the cars and motorcycles more directly than pedestrians and bus riders.
findings.caveats: Not tested in the study. Discussion: motorcyclists 'are exposed to exhaust from other motor vehicles as well as their own motorcycles, especially during busy traffic hours' citing other work [27,29,63]. No analysis of which vehicles were ahead; routes were thoroughfares.
findings.useOnSite: The authors suggest riders sit in the car lanes and take in exhaust from nearby cars and motorcycles, but they did not measure which vehicles produced it.
findings.checkerNote: Both quotes verified.

findings.claim: The paper states, citing other work, that motorcycle traffic contributes to roadside PM2.5.
findings.value: Qualitative, cited
findings.quote: Motorcycle traffic contributes to roadside PM2.5 [28,29,62].
findings.caveats: Only a cited assertion; the paper gives no tailpipe emission data and never says 'gasoline', 'scooter' or fuel type, and measures no benzene, CO or hydrocarbons.
findings.useOnSite: The authors cite earlier work saying motorcycle traffic adds to roadside PM2.5.
findings.checkerNote: Verified; word search confirms absence of scooter/gasoline/fuel/benzene in the body.

findings.claim: The authors report more than 3 million motorcycles in the Taipei and New Taipei area as of 31 May 2019.
findings.value: More than 3 million motorcycles (Taipei City + New Taipei City), 31 May 2019
findings.quote: as of 31 May 2019, there are more than 3 million motorcycles in the metropolitan Taipei area
findings.caveats: Cited from Ministry data [64]; population given on p.2 as 2,663,425 and 3,998,883 (31 Mar 2019). The paper says 'Taiwan Ministry of Traffic and Communication'. The paper says numbers have risen 'steadily' over the decade but gives no earlier count.
findings.useOnSite: The authors note over 3 million motorcycles in the Taipei metro area in mid-2019.
findings.checkerNote: Verified; 'and rising' dropped from the claim since no figures are given.

findings.claim: The authors estimate a delivery rider (UberEATS example) could inhale more than 46 mg of PM2.5 a year.
findings.value: More than 46 mg/yr (8 h/day, 5 days/week on a motorcycle, minute ventilation 5 L/min)
findings.quote: the person may inhale the cumulative exposure to PM2.5 a year would be more than 46 mg a year, assuming a minute ventilation of 5 L/min
findings.caveats: Uses the idle (red-light) concentration for all hours, an unadjusted sensor reading (about 30% high), and resting ventilation; authors say moving exposure is 'probably' lower. The concentration used is not printed. Checker arithmetic: 75 ug/m3 x 0.3 m3/h x 8 h x 5 d x 52 wk is about 47 mg, consistent with 46.
findings.useOnSite: The authors' rough estimate is over 46 mg PM2.5 inhaled per year by a full-time delivery rider, assuming idle-level air throughout; they say true exposure may be lower.
findings.checkerNote: Quote and assumptions verified; arithmetic reproduced.

findings.claim: Air-conditioned bus interiors were lower than walking; roadside bus stops were higher than inside the bus.
findings.value: Bus: median 35 ug/m3, range 13-65, n = 38; p = 0.0025 vs walking
findings.quote: The median PM2.5 concentration inside the buses was 35 µg/m3 (range: 13–65 µg/m3 , n = 38 measurements), lower than that of walking (p = 0.0025).
findings.caveats: All buses had AC on; only 38 readings. Bus-stop values are described only qualitatively in the text. In Fig. 6 (1 May, drizzle, RH 87%) the bus-station points are roughly 27-35 against roughly 15-25 inside the bus (read from figure, approximate).
findings.useOnSite: Inside AC buses the median was 35 ug/m3 versus 40 walking; at roadside bus stops it was higher than inside the bus.
findings.checkerNote: Verified; added approximate Fig. 6 values.

findings.claim: Closed, air-conditioned car cabins had the lowest median.
findings.value: Car: median 15 ug/m3, range 8-80, n = 111, p<0.0001 vs walking (5 trips)
findings.quote: There were five car trips. The PM2.5 concentrations were lower compared to those during walking (median: 15 µg/m3 ; range: 8–80 µg/m3 , n = 111 measurements, p < 0.0001 vs. walking).
findings.caveats: Drivers were asked to use AC, recirculation, windows closed (p.4); a protective condition not typical of all car use. Five trips only. Occupant exposure, not pedestrian.
findings.useOnSite: Inside a closed air-conditioned car the median was 15 ug/m3, showing enclosure matters; pedestrians and riders have no such shield.
findings.checkerNote: Verified.

findings.claim: Underground MRT stations and cars were the highest commute modes, about twice walking.
findings.value: Underground stations: median 75 (text; abstract says 80), range 30-210, n = 92; underground cars: median 80, range 53-185 (abstract 55-185), n = 188; both p<0.0001 vs walking. 34 MRT trips
findings.quote: the median concentrations of PM2.5 in the stations and in the metro cars were 75 µg/m3 (range: 30–210 µg/m3 , n = 92 measurements) and 80 µg/m3 (range: 53–185 µg/m3 , n = 188 measurements), respectively.
findings.caveats: Abstract and text disagree for station median (80 vs 75) and car range lower bound (55 vs 53). Discussion says '75 and 80'. Sensor overestimate applies. MRT is electric rail, not an electric scooter; the elevated MRT results are low, the underground results high.
findings.useOnSite: Underground MRT medians were about 75-80 ug/m3, similar to the paper's idle-motorcycle figure; the paper's cause is rail-wear particles and poor ventilation, so it says nothing about electric scooters.
findings.checkerNote: Numbers confirmed. useOnSite reworded: reader's 'does not show electric transport is uniformly cleaner' risks implying a result about electric scooters or tailpipe removal; the paper tests neither.

findings.claim: Elevated (above-ground) MRT stations and cars were much lower than underground, and lower than walking.
findings.value: Elevated stations: median 33, range 15-35, n = 10 (p<0.0001 vs underground stations; p = 0.0025 vs walking). Elevated cars: median 20 (text; abstract says 28), range 13-68, n = 52 (p<0.0001 vs underground trains and vs walking)
findings.quote: median: 33 µg/m3 ; range: 15–35 µg/m3 , n = 10 measurements ... median: 20 µg/m3 ; range: 13–68 µg/m3 , n = 52 measurements
findings.caveats: Elevated cars median is 20 in the text but 28 in the abstract; the Fig. 8 box looks about 25. Station n = 10 is small. Fig. 5 shows concentrations falling to about 12-22 once the train rose out of the tunnel (27 Apr, RH 84%).
findings.useOnSite: Electric trains on elevated track recorded about 20-33 ug/m3 in the same study, lower than walking.
findings.checkerNote: Verified in text and Fig. 5.

findings.claim: The authors attribute high underground MRT PM2.5 to rail/wheel/brake wear plus inadequate ventilation, not tailpipes.
findings.value: Qualitative; compares underground vs elevated
findings.quote: Although electric-powered, MRT generates its own air pollutants due to abrasion and wear of rail tracks, wheels and braking pads ... suggests that inadequate ventilation plays an important role.
findings.caveats: Composition not measured in this study; iron-rich composition is cited from other cities (p.10). Non-exhaust particles in an enclosed space.
findings.useOnSite: Electric trains are not particle-free underground, where wear particles and poor ventilation raise PM2.5; the authors say this is not tailpipe-related.
findings.checkerNote: Verified pp.2, 10, 12.

findings.claim: The authors estimate an MRT rider could inhale over 8 mg PM2.5 a year.
findings.value: More than 8 mg/yr (1 h/day in MRT, 5 L/min)
findings.quote: the rider may inhale more than 8 mg of PM2.5 a year from MRT alone [55]
findings.caveats: Uses uncorrected readings; resting ventilation (authors: riders were stationary).
findings.useOnSite: For comparison with the 46 mg delivery-rider estimate, the authors give about 8 mg/yr for an hour a day on underground MRT.
findings.checkerNote: Verified; 75 ug/m3 x 0.3 m3/h x 365 h is about 8 mg.

findings.claim: A 2008 Taipei study (Tsai et al., cited) found the same mode ordering except for MRT, with motorcyclists highest.
findings.value: Tsai 2008 as quoted: motorcycle 67.5, bus 38.5, MRT 35, car 22.1 ug/m3
findings.quote: motorcyclists had the highest exposure (67.5 µg/m3 ) followed by bus riders (38.5 µg/m3 ), MRT riders (35 µg/m3 ) and car drivers (22.1 µg/m3 )
findings.caveats: Different study and instrument. The authors say motorcycle exposure 'remained high' compared with 2008; they do not claim a statistical comparison.
findings.useOnSite: The authors say a 2008 Taipei study also found motorcyclists with the highest commute exposure.
findings.checkerNote: Verified; the ordering sentence is on p.12.

findings.claim: Fig. 8 box plots show the ranking of all modes.
findings.value: Higher than walking along roadside (*): underground MRT stations, underground MRT cars, motorcycle. Lower than walking (§): private cars, buses. Underground higher than elevated (#)
findings.quote: MRT station (underground), MRT car (underground) and motorcycle were higher than walking along roadside (*) ... Private cars and buses are lower than walking along the roadside (§).
findings.caveats: Elevated MRT stations/cars are described as lower than walking in the text but are not marked § in the figure.
findings.useOnSite: See the paper's Figure 8 for a side-by-side of all modes.
findings.checkerNote: Verified on PDF page 10.

findings.claim: Several example trips were done at humidity levels near or beyond the sensor's validated range.
findings.value: Example trip humidity: 11 Jun RH 99% (Fig. 4); 27 Apr RH 84% (Fig. 5); 1 May RH 87% drizzle (Fig. 6); 29 Apr RH 69% (Fig. 7); walks 10 Apr RH 69% (Table 1) and 77% (Table 2). Sensor spec RH 0-90%; authors: RH >80% may overestimate; 'minimal effect' up to 65% RH
findings.quote: High relative humidity (>80%) may result in overestimation of PM2.5 concentration [67].
findings.caveats: Authors argue climate had 'minimal effect' per tests of the sensor, but note the 65% RH limit in Methods; the motorcycle example (RH 69%) was the driest of the four trip figures (Table 1 walk was also 69%) yet still above 65%.
findings.useOnSite: Humid-day readings in the paper may be biased high; the authors say so.
findings.checkerNote: Corrected 'driest' claim (Table 1 walk also 69%) and added Table 1/2 humidity.

findings.claim: The authors cite other work that ground-level PM2.5 is much higher than at elevated monitors.
findings.value: PM2.5 below 10 m 10 to 20 times higher than in high-rise buildings, especially near busy roads; black carbon underestimated 4-9x by monitoring sites; black carbon walking/cycling up to 6x bus
findings.quote: Outdoor PM2.5 concentrations below the height of 10-m buildings (three-story) were 10 to 20 times greater than those found at higher high-rise buildings, especially near busy roads [30].
findings.caveats: Not measured here. This paper's own street-vs-station results are much smaller than 10-20x (roughly 2-4x in the examples).
findings.useOnSite: Do not cite 10-20x as this paper's finding; it is quoted from another study.
findings.checkerNote: Verified.

findings.claim: The introduction cites mortality estimates for PM exposure from earlier work.
findings.value: Daily cardiopulmonary mortality +0.3% per 10 ug/m3 PM10; long-term cardiopulmonary mortality +6% per 10 ug/m3 annual PM2.5 (cited Pope 2002 [5])
findings.quote: daily cardiopulmonary mortality rose by 0.3% for each 10-µg/m3 increase in PM10 ... the estimate was 6% for each 10-µg/m3 increase in annual average exposure to PM2.5
findings.significance: No CI given in this paper.
findings.caveats: Not a result of this study; long-term average ambient exposure, not commuting peaks. No health outcomes in the paper.
findings.useOnSite: Cite Pope 2002 directly for the 6% figure rather than this paper.
findings.checkerNote: Verified.

findings.claim: The introduction names the elderly and people with chronic lung/heart disease as at particular risk, citing other work.
findings.value: Qualitative
findings.quote: The risk is especially high in the elderly and patients with chronic obstructive lung disease, asthma, coronary artery disease, congestive heart failure and cardiac arrhythmias [12–17].
findings.caveats: The study measured no children, strollers, elderly or health outcomes. Volunteers' ages/heights not given; sensor held at adult mid-chest height. The word 'children' appears only in a reference title.
findings.useOnSite: The paper itself offers no data on children or older people.
findings.checkerNote: Quote fixed: paper says 'chronic obstructive lung disease', reader wrote 'pulmonary'.

findings.claim: The authors flag delivery riders and food-stall workers as high-exposure groups needing health studies, noting none exist.
findings.value: Qualitative
findings.quote: There have been no health studies on these subpopulations.
findings.caveats: The closing sentence (p.12) names the underground food-court workers; delivery riders are raised on p.11 as 'at higher risk'. Based on temple/food-court readings and idle motorcycle readings; no health outcomes.
findings.useOnSite: The authors call for studies of food-stall workers and say delivery riders may be at higher risk; exposure is high but unstudied.
findings.checkerNote: Verified; quote is p.12.

findings.claim: Authors conclude some commuting modes, notably underground MRT and motorcycle, entail high PM2.5, and motorcycle exposure exceeded elevated MRT.
findings.value: Qualitative
findings.quote: The exposure for the motorcyclists is also higher compare to the MRT riders when the train on the elevated outdoor tracks.
findings.caveats: Main hypothesis was about MRT riders (p.2); motorcycle comparisons rest on 3 trips of idle readings.
findings.useOnSite: The authors conclude motorcycle exposure stayed high compared with 2008 despite MRT expansion.
findings.checkerNote: Verified.

findings.claim: Indoor readings in the example trips were themselves well above the simultaneous station values, so part of the street-minus-station gap is not street-specific.
findings.value: Table 1 (ambient 21): hospital 1st floor 65, office 57.5. Table 2 (ambient 5): inside house 20. Fig. 7 (stations 17-20): indoor 35 before and about 55 after the ride. Fig. 4 (stations 2, 6): indoor about 8. Fig. 6: indoor about 15
findings.quote: Table 1: Hospital 1st floor | 65; Office in the hospital | 57.5
findings.caveats: Reading from tables and approximate figure values; the paper does not discuss this. Consistent with the authors' own statement that the sensor overestimates, but could also reflect indoor sources.
findings.useOnSite: Do not present street-versus-station multiples as pure traffic effects; the paper's own indoor readings were also above station values.
findings.checkerNote: Checker observation drawn from the paper's tables and figures; not stated by the authors.

findings.claim: Fig. 7 shows the motorcycle trip rose from an indoor reading of about 35 to about 75, roughly double, and about 4x the nearby stations (17-20); 'several fold' is relative to the stations.
findings.value: Fig. 7 (29 Apr, partly cloudy, 29 C, RH 69%): indoor about 35 at 18:26, then about 75 at 18:44 with no points between; ride points about 60-75; stations 20, 17, 20
findings.quote: The PM2.5 concentration increased quickly by several fold after the ride began.
findings.caveats: Figure values are read from the plot (approximate). The line between 18:26 and 18:44 is interpolation. Only idle readings were taken, so the rise cannot be tied to a specific event such as a red light.
findings.useOnSite: The authors say concentrations rose 'several fold' when the ride began; in the plot this is about 2x the indoor reading and about 4x the nearby stations.
findings.checkerNote: Reader quoted the sentence only in answer 4 without the figure context.

findings.claim: The authors state that walking along streets was exposed to higher PM2.5 than riding air-conditioned cars and buses, and give traffic density and AC as likely reasons.

limitations: Hand-held optical detector may be influenced by co-responsive pollutants, humidity (>80% may overestimate) and unit variation; it 'was shown to overestimate', correction about 30% downward; results unadjusted (pp.3, 12).
Not calibrated against FEM-GRIMM or TEOM ('not available to us'); only a room-air check of 5-10 ug/m3 before each trip (p.3).
Detector not used in previous transport studies; drift said to be minimal because the study was short (p.12).
Low-wind conditions only; April-July 2019 only, the lowest ambient season (p.3), so annual exposure is not represented.
Motorcycle PM2.5 measured only while idle; moving exposure is 'difficult to measure' and 'probably' lower (pp.4, 11).
Small samples: 3 motorcycle trips (21 readings), 5 car trips, 10 elevated-station readings. Authors argue motorcycle data are 'representative' because spread was small (p.11).
Five volunteers (chosen to reduce inter-observer variability, p.3); one detector. Per-volunteer data and the motorcycle used are not reported. Readings are repeated within trips, not independent.
No adjustment for time of day, traffic counts, wind or rain; only pooled rank-sum comparisons.
No logging interval beyond 1-min resolution; total hours per mode not given.
Poor station-street correlation (R2 = 0.275) and differing methods acknowledged (p.5).
No other pollutants, no health outcomes, no tailpipe or fuel data, no data on children, older people or strollers.
complications: Underground electric MRT (median 75-80) was as high as the idle motorcycle (75): high PM2.5 occurs in electric rail too, from wear particles and poor ventilation. This says nothing about electric scooters and should not be used for or against link 7.
Motorcycle median 75 comes from 3 trips and idle readings only; it is not riding-in-motion exposure, and the authors think moving exposure is lower.
The paper never says whether motorcycles were gasoline, never uses 'scooter', never mentions electric motorcycles.

The only walking peaks attributed to a source are temple incense and cooking; the sidewalk maximum of 275 is unexplained. Intersection rises are attributed to 'automobile traffic' and road dust, not scooters or red lights.
Walking median (40) is only modestly above bus (35); elevated MRT stations (33) and cars (20) are below walking.

By the authors' reasoning all sensor values are about 30% high; the adjusted equation would put the walking median near 30 and motorcycle near 54 (checker arithmetic, not in paper). Authors argue relative differences are unaffected.
No evidence on children, strollers or older people, and no health outcomes: links 5 and 6 rest on other literature.
Season was the lowest-pollution period (station median 14); the paper does not say whether winter street exposure is higher.
Indoor readings in the example trips (e.g. 57.5 and 65 in Table 1, ambient 21) are also well above station values, so street-minus-station gaps are not purely traffic.
Street-vs-station relation is weak (R2 0.275); the cited 10-20x height gradient is far above the roughly 2-4x seen in the examples.
Annual dose figures (8 mg, 46 mg) assume resting 5 L/min ventilation and idle-state concentrations, so they are crude.

Internal inconsistencies: motorcycle p<0.0001 (abstract) vs 0.0011 (text); station median 80 vs 75; underground car lower bound 55 vs 53; elevated MRT car median 28 vs 20; station inlet height 15-20 m (p.4) vs 10-15 m (pp.2, 5, 12); Tables 1 and 2 both dated 10 April but described as sunny and rainy; text cites time points 15:20 and 15:25 not in Table 3.

answersToQuestions: 1. Design: five volunteers, one Temtop P600 laser light-scattering detector held at mid-chest height, sensor facing away; 1-min time resolution, 3 readings averaged per measurement; low wind only (pp.3-4). April to July 2019 only (p.4), the lowest-ambient months. Trips: 34 MRT trips (30-90 min; rush and off-peak), 3 motorcycle trips, 5 car trips; bus and walking trip counts and hours per mode not stated. Not calibrated against a reference; authors cite a manufacturer field test (adjusted = 0.678 x measured + 3.298, R2 0.915, about 30% downward, intra-model variability about 7%) and a room-air check of 5-10 ug/m3 before each trip (p.3). Results unadjusted.

2. Table A in chartReady: walking 40 (10-275, n=216); underground stations 75 (30-210, n=92); underground cars 80 (53-185, n=188); elevated stations 33 (15-35, n=10); elevated cars 20 (13-68, n=52); bus 35 (13-65, n=38); motorcycle 75 (60-105, n=21); car 15 (8-80, n=111). No means given for modes. Walking sub-categories: only means +/- SD near temples (588 +/- 271) and underground food court (405 +/- 238), n not stated; single readings in example walks (Tables 1-3); no separate statistics for intersections, arcades or parks.

3. The 275 maximum is not attributed to any source, place or time; Fig. 8 shows roadside outliers from about 135 to 275. Sources are named only for temple readings ('if one walks by temples, the PM2.5 concentration can increase many folds due to incent burning', p.11) and food stalls ('inadequate ventilation', p.11). Intersections: 'increased automobile traffic that generated more exhaust and road dust' (p.5). The paper never mentions scooters, smoking or cigarettes; 'red lights' appears only in the motorcycle idle protocol (p.4), not in any walking analysis.

4. Readings were taken only while idle, 'for example, waiting for red lights' (p.4), at 'different stops' on thoroughfares (p.11). 'In Taiwan, motorcyclists frequently ride on the car lanes. Therefore, they would be exposed to exhaust from the cars and motorcycles more directly than pedestrians and bus riders' (p.8); riders are exposed to 'exhaust from other motor vehicles as well as their own motorcycles' (p.11, citing others). Fig. 7: 'increased quickly by several fold after the ride began' (about 2x the indoor 35, about 4x the stations). No data on vehicles ahead; moving exposure assumed 'probably' lower (p.11).

5. 24 paired measurements at five stations: S = 0.958 M + 23.353, R2 = 0.275, p = 0.006 (p.5); street about 12-55 vs station about 2-22 (Fig. 2). No ratio reported. Example trips: motorcycle about 60-75 vs 17-20 (Fig. 7); bus 15-35 vs 4-10 (Fig. 6); underground MRT 70-95 vs 2 and 6 (Fig. 4); Table 1 walk ambient 21 vs 57.5-100; Table 3 walk ambient 5 vs 30-700. 'Most PM2.5 measurements during commuting were higher than the ambient concentrations' (p.12), attributed to sensor overestimate plus vertical gradient and method differences. Indoor readings were also above station values in several examples.

6. Authors: PM from 'abrasion and wear of rail tracks, wheels and braking pads' (pp.2, 10) and 'inadequate ventilation' (p.12), inferred from lower readings on elevated sections and the drop when the train emerged (Fig. 5). Iron-rich composition cited from other cities (p.10); composition not measured here. A prior Taipei platform study of 75.4 (winter) and 56.2 (summer) ug/m3 is cited (p.10).

7. Quotes: 'the measured PM2.5 concentrations will need to be adjusted downward by about 30%' (p.3); 'The detector was not calibrated against FEM-GRIMM or ... TEOM since they were not available to us' (p.3); 'although our detector could overestimate the absolute values of PM2.5, the relative changes and the direction of the changes would not be affected' (p.12); 'We used a small number of volunteers to decrease the interobserver variability' (p.3). Conclusions (p.12): 'our study found subgroups of residents in the Taipei metropolitan area who may be exposed to high concentrations of PM2.5'; 'The exposure for the motorcyclists remained high compared to a previous study in 2008'; 'There have been no health studies on these subpopulations.' The authors do not list sample size or single detector as limitations in so many words.

8. Only PM2.5 was measured. Other pollutants appear only in cited background: black carbon (underestimated 4-9x by monitoring sites; walking/cycling up to 6x bus, p.2) and iron, carbon and other components of subway PM (p.10). No CO, benzene, hydrocarbons, NOx or ultrafine data; no tailpipe emission data.
